inhalt:
This article addresses the question of what is meant by parametric or algorithmic design in architecture. Often these terms merely serve to characterize avant-garde-looking designs that were created or realized with computer support. Since such a very general use of the terms is not fruitful for the topic discussed here, an examination of the technical foundations seems necessary.

Before we turn to various computer-based design methods, we must therefore recall how physical objects are represented in the computer by means of a geometric model. A geometric model represents certain elements such as points, edges, faces and volumes. In terms of data, these elements are represented primarily by their properties, e.g., their coordinates describing their position. From a technical point of view, there are at least five different representation schemes for geometric models, but these need not concern us further here. What matters is that every form of representation requires information on certain element properties, which at this level can be regarded as parameter values. From this perspective, every geometric model is also a parametric model.

The decisive question here is how the user of a computer program can create (model) geometric elements and subsequently access (manipulate) them. The functionality of classic CAD programs was conceived primarily as a replication of drawing on a drawing board, as was customary among engineers. In today's common software, this means that the element parameters are usually accessed either through the user's graphical interaction with the geometric objects displayed on screen via mouse input (indirectly) or through the numerical entry of new property values for specific elements (directly). We can therefore speak of software for parametric modeling as soon as it enables a user to create and manipulate geometric elements directly and indirectly. It is also worth noting that the user interaction described usually refers to geometric objects composed of several geometric elements. A cuboid, for example, consists of 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces. Manipulating the height of a cuboid automatically affects the coordinate values of some of these sub-elements.

If a geometric model is created in such a way that dependencies (associativities) exist between the geometric elements or their parameters, it is called an associative model. Such a model is usually structured hierarchically, so that the dependencies or connections between the elements are organized in a tree structure. As a consequence of this structure, all elements build on a first, “primordial” element, and changes to this first element affect all the others.

Associative models run into difficulties with network-like associativity, in which elements are in a circular dependency on one another. Such interconnection is difficult to handle because of the complexity it entails and requires certain control mechanisms that precisely define the conditions of interaction between two elements. Such a definition has to be specified by means of algorithms, which is why network-like associative models have to be supplemented with special methods. The distinction drawn between geometric and associative models gives rise to different possibilities for their use in the architectural design process. We distinguish between methods of parametric and of algorithmic design.

Parametric design is primarily concerned with the associative linking of the parameters of different geometric objects in order to represent complicated dependencies organized in a tree structure. Algorithmic design takes network-like parameter linkages into account, which can lead to interactions and feedback between geometric objects. Since feedback processes play an important role in complex systems, these can only be represented by means of algorithmic design methods.

Algorithmic design requires sound knowledge of programming techniques, which are difficult to teach in architectural education because they demand strictly logical and mathematical thinking that at first glance seems to contradict creative work on architectural designs. Presumably for this reason, computational design initiatives failed to become established; in the 1990s they were tried out in various educational programs at experimentally oriented universities worldwide and dealt with the development of small, custom computer programs for specific design tasks. The technical basis for this work was usually provided by scripting languages, e.g., AutoLisp or VBA for AutoCAD. In recent years, however, a trend can be observed that, starting from the MIT Media Lab and protagonists such as John Maeda, understands programming as a fundamental design method. This trend has led to programming courses increasingly being integrated into the education of designers and architects.

The concept of parametric modeling was first implemented in software for mechanical engineering, industrial design (Pro/Engineer) and film production (Maya, 3D Studio Max). In the field of CAAD software, the parameterization of geometric objects gave rise to component-based modeling, in which the dimensions of building components such as doors, windows or walls can be controlled via parameters. Current developments in architecture push the concept of parameterization to its limits under the label Building Information Modeling (BIM), by assigning every conceivable property to building components (e.g., cost, materiality, insulation values) and attempting to represent the structure of buildings in universally valid schemes (e.g., number of stories, facade build-up, roof construction). The aim of the BIM approach is to combine all building-related information in one digital model, which is intended to increase efficiency in building planning and construction. The problem with this approach is that the essence of creative design is to continually evade prefabricated schemes and to seek unconventional paths, which the relatively rigid BIM systems often make difficult or even impossible to pursue.

As an alternative to CAAD and BIM systems (e.g., Revit, Allplan, ArchiCAD), relatively flexible 3D modeling programs for architectural applications have been developed that forgo the potential of the BIM approach and are less suited to drawing plans or construction details, but in return offer great freedom in formal design. One of these programs is Rhino3D, which has been available since the late 1990s and has now established itself as very affordable modeling software (compared with established programs in this field such as Cinema 4D, 3ds Max or Maya).

Numerous architecture-specific plugins exist for Rhino3D. In the present discussion, we focus on the Grasshopper plugin, which has been developed mainly by David Rutten since 2007. Grasshopper can be used to create complicated models that are ideally suited to parametric design. For parametric modeling, Grasshopper offers a graphical editor that makes it possible to define parameter dependencies between groups of elements and to link these dependencies with predefined or user-created algorithms.

With some effort, Grasshopper also makes it possible to define circular dependencies between geometric elements. The plugin is therefore also suitable, to a limited extent, for algorithmic design. In any case, it is one of the first and, above all, most user-friendly systems that allow abstract definitions for associative models to be created with very little programming knowledge and primarily by graphical means. Not least because of its intuitive graphical user interface and its many possibilities for experimentation, Grasshopper is very popular among architecture students. The connection to Rhino3D allows the generated geometry to be further manipulated with conventional CAD functions.

Owing to the inherent logic of parametric modeling, the geometry generated with Grasshopper is usually very complicated and can only be realized with the help of digital fabrication methods. For this reason, new generative software systems and new digital fabrication techniques have been driving each other forward in recent years. To take account of this development, the teaching of digital fabrication processes is increasingly being integrated into university curricula.
